# Federal Compliance for Moderate Agencies {.unnumbered}

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**[Download this whitepaper as DOCX](federal-compliance-for-moderate-agencies.docx)** — a Word copy of
this page, regenerated on every site deploy. (Also available from the
**Other Formats** link in the page sidebar.)
:::
:::

## The problem this paper resolves

Every mandate in this space — FedRAMP, NIST SP 800-53, CISA's directives,
OMB's memos, TIC 3.0 — gets discussed as if it applies to "the government"
undifferentiated. It doesn't. Some of these bind a **Cloud Service Provider**
seeking or keeping an authorization to sell into the federal market. Some
bind a **federal agency** operating its own systems, whether on-premises or
on top of an authorized cloud. A few bind both, in different ways, at
different points in the same supply chain. Conflating the two produces two
opposite failure modes this paper exists to prevent: agencies that assume
"FedRAMP" is someone else's problem and miss their own continuous-monitoring
obligation, and agencies that pour effort into vendor-shaped compliance
work — chasing a CSP's authorization paperwork — that was never theirs to do.

This paper answers one question per mandate — **who does this actually
bind?** — states the deadlines that matter, and then gets out of the way:
every mandate below is covered in far more depth by a companion whitepaper
in this section, and this page's job is to route you to the right one, not
to re-derive what they already establish. **Scope:** federal civilian
agencies operating at the FedRAMP Moderate baseline (GCC-Moderate for
Microsoft 365 tenants specifically). DoD/IL4-IL5, state and local, and
commercial-non-federal compliance regimes are out of scope — see [Honest
limits](#honest-limits-and-scope).

## Executive summary

Three distinct actors sit inside "federal compliance," and almost every
mandate below binds exactly one of them directly:

| Actor | Role | Directly bound by |
|---|---|---|
| **Cloud Service Provider (CSP) / vendor** | Builds and operates a Cloud Service Offering (CSO) it sells into the federal market | FedRAMP (the baseline itself, and the 20x Consolidated Rules specifically) |
| **Federal agency** (AO, ISSO, CISO, mission owner) | Operates systems — its own, or built on top of an authorized CSO — and holds its own Authority to Operate | NIST SP 800-53/800-37 (its own ATO), CISA's directives (BOD 25-01, the Zero Trust Maturity Model), OMB's policy memos (M-22-09, M-25-21, M-19-26/TIC 3.0) |
| **Independent assessor (3PAO, or an agency's own assessment function)** | Validates either side's evidence | Whichever framework it's assessing against — FedRAMP's assessment requirements for a CSP, or the agency's own RMF/ATO process for agency-operated systems |

The confusion is that FedRAMP 20x's headline change — continuous,
machine-readable evidence instead of periodic assessment — is a **CSP-facing
authorization requirement**, but the same evidentiary bar (continuous,
machine-readable, not point-in-time) is *also* rising for agencies' own
systems under NIST SP 800-37's continuous-monitoring requirement (CA-7) and
OMB Circular A-130. An agency reading "FedRAMP 20x" and concluding "not my
problem, that's a CSP thing" misses that its own ATO package is being held
to the same rising bar, on a different legal basis, on roughly the same
timeline. That's the distinction this paper exists to make explicit.

## 1. FedRAMP and the 20x Consolidated Rules — binds vendors directly; agencies inherit the evidence

**Who it binds:** FedRAMP authorizes Cloud Service Offerings. The
Consolidated Rules — published June 25, 2026 — are requirements a **CSP**
meets to obtain and keep that authorization: machine-readable Key Security
Indicators (KSIs), submitted through one of three certification pipelines,
replacing the prior periodic-assessment model.

**What it means for agencies:** an agency does not submit into the FedRAMP
20x pipeline the way a CSP does. What changes for the agency is what it can
now *expect to receive*: continuous KSI evidence from its FedRAMP-authorized
cloud providers instead of a stale point-in-time assessment package, and a
narrower window in which an older-style (Rev5) authorization remains valid
at all. An agency's own procurement and ATO-reciprocity decisions — which
CSOs it relies on, and how it cites that reliance in its own SSP — depend on
tracking these dates:

- **June 25, 2026** — FedRAMP publishes the Consolidated Rules for 2026;
  the machine-readable KSI evidence regime is defined.
- **July 6, 2026** — 20x Marketplace listings open; CSPs may enter the
  initial implementation stage.
- **July 28, 2026** — FedRAMP Ready submissions cease; no new Ready pathway.
- **August 3, 2026** — Class A pipeline opens (first new-authorization
  submission window).
- **August 10, 2026** — Temporary Rev5 Program Certification opens
  (Class B/C Ready-conversion and lost-sponsor paths).
- **August 31, 2026** — Class B and C pipelines open — Class C (Moderate)
  is the class the CSOs a Moderate-baseline agency actually relies on
  (M365 GCC, GovCloud, DDI providers) will enter. This is the pipeline
  your vendors submit into; it is not an agency submission window.
- **December 7, 2026** — FedRAMP's Vulnerability Detection & Response
  (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation & Reporting (VER) rules become
  mandatory, aligned to CISA BOD 26-04's remediation timelines taking
  effect the same date (see [§4](#bod-26-04)).
- **January 1, 2027** — Consolidated Rules mandatory for all certified
  systems; the legacy Rev5 path closes for new authorizations.
- **June 11, 2027** — no new Rev5 certifications accepted.

**What it means for vendors:** everything above is the actual compliance
work. A CSP not moving toward Consolidated-Rules certification on this
timeline risks losing the ability to sell to federal agencies at all once
Rev5 stops being issued.

**Read deeper:** [Federal Application Aware Networking
Architecture](federal-application-aware-networking-architecture.qmd) §
"FedRAMP 20x Consolidated Rules" covers the KSI evidence-format mechanics
and a worked Call to Action built around these dates. For the full
control-by-control mapping and the fuller federal compliance clock this
timeline is drawn from, see the [OrgComp series' Executive
Summary](../orgcomp-series/Vol_0_Book_00_OrgComp_Executive_Summary.qmd)
("FedRAMP 20x Hard Deadlines" and "The Broader Federal Clock").

## 2. NIST SP 800-53 / SP 800-37 (the Risk Management Framework) — binds agencies directly for systems they operate

**Who it binds:** any federal agency operating an information system,
regardless of where it runs (on-premises, in an authorized CSP's cloud, or
hybrid). The agency's Authorizing Official (AO) issues and owns the Authority
to Operate (ATO) under NIST SP 800-37's Risk Management Framework, against
the control baseline NIST SP 800-53 defines (Moderate baseline, for the
GCC-Moderate scope this paper covers).

**What it means for agencies:** this is the mandate most directly "yours" of
everything in this paper. Running on top of a FedRAMP-authorized CSO
inherits that CSO's own controls but does **not** relieve the agency of its
own ATO for the system it built on top of it — a common point of confusion
this paper exists partly to close. NIST SP 800-37's CA-7 continuous-monitoring
requirement is the agency-side analog of FedRAMP 20x's KSI evidence — same
"continuous, not periodic" shift, different legal basis (the agency's own
RMF obligation, not a CSP's FedRAMP authorization).

**What it means for vendors:** a CSP's FedRAMP authorization is an input to
an agency's risk decision, not a substitute for the agency completing its
own ATO. A vendor selling "FedRAMP authorized" as if it closes the agency's
compliance work oversells what the authorization covers.

**Read deeper:** every whitepaper in this section that cites specific NIST
SP 800-53 controls (SC-7, SC-8, AC-4, SI-3, CM-8, and others) is doing RMF
work for a specific domain — see the [routing
table](#where-to-read-deeper-by-mandate) for which paper covers which
control family. For the full authorization-package mechanics — the OSCAL
bundle, the KSI scorecard, and how continuous evidence actually assembles
into an AP/AR/POA&M set — see the [OrgComp series' Authorization Package
and ConMon
book](../orgcomp-series/Vol_IV_Book_06_OrgComp_Authorization_Package_ConMon.qmd).

## 3. CISA Binding Operational Directive 25-01 (SCuBA) — binds agencies directly, on a fixed timeline

**Who it binds:** federal civilian executive branch agencies operating
Microsoft 365 tenants. [BOD
25-01](https://cyber.dhs.gov/bod/25-01/), *Implementing Secure Practices for
Cloud Services*, requires agencies to identify their M365 tenants, implement
CISA's SCuBA Secure Configuration Baselines against them, deploy the
ScubaGear assessment tool, integrate with CISA's continuous-monitoring
infrastructure, and **remediate deviations** from the baselines — not merely
report them. Tenant identification was due February 21, 2025; ScubaGear
deployment followed on a subsequent deadline.

**What it means for agencies:** this directive is unambiguously agency-facing
— there is no vendor party BOD 25-01 binds. The remediation clause is the
part agencies most often under-invest in: running the assessor and reporting
findings satisfies the letter of "assess," but not "remediate deviations,"
and a growing, un-closed deviation list is not a defensible posture under the
directive's own text.

**What it means for vendors:** Microsoft (as the M365 platform owner) and any
third-party tooling vendor selling into this space are not directly bound by
BOD 25-01 — the directive's obligations run to the agency operating the
tenant, not to the platform or tool vendor.

**Read deeper:** [Assessment Tools vs. Closing BOD-25-01
Findings](bod-25-01-close-before-assess.qmd) is this paper's dedicated
treatment of the directive, including why "run the assessor" and "close the
findings" are different obligations and the correct sequencing between them.
[ScubaGear Integration](scubagear-integration-whitepaper.qmd) and [ZTA and
SCuBA — How They Relate](zta-scuba-relationship.qmd) cover the tooling layer
this directive requires.

## 4. CISA BOD 26-04 (risk-based vulnerability remediation) — binds agencies directly {#bod-26-04}

**Who it binds:** federal civilian executive branch agencies. BOD 26-04,
issued June 10, 2026, replaces flat CVSS-severity remediation windows with a
four-variable risk model — exposure, presence on CISA's Known Exploited
Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, whether the vulnerability is automatable, and
mission impact — producing remediation timelines that range from three days
for the highest-risk combination down to a deferral path for genuinely
low-risk findings. It supersedes the older, cruder "CVSS 9+ closes in 15
days" style of policy still common in agency vulnerability-management SOPs.

**What it means for agencies:** two concrete dates matter. Agency
vulnerability-management policy has to support the four-variable, risk-based
remediation model by **August 7, 2026**; the remediation timelines
themselves take legal effect **December 7, 2026**, the same date FedRAMP's
own VDR/VER (Vulnerability Detection & Response / Vulnerability Evaluation
& Reporting) rules become mandatory for CSPs (§1). An agency's existing
BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation) program is the closest predecessor process —
BOD 26-04 doesn't replace BOD 22-01's KEV-catalog obligation, it adds the
exposure/automatability/impact variables on top of it.

**What it means for vendors:** a CSP's own VDR/VER disclosure obligations
under FedRAMP (§1) are the vendor-side mirror of this directive — a
vulnerability an agency has to risk-score and remediate against BOD 26-04's
clock is frequently one a vendor is separately obligated to have already
disclosed. The two obligations run on the same December 7, 2026 date for
exactly that reason.

**Read deeper:** this directive is new enough that no whitepaper in this
section yet carries a dedicated treatment — [Assessment Tools vs. Closing
BOD-25-01 Findings](bod-25-01-close-before-assess.qmd)'s remediate-before-assess
sequencing argument applies directly to BOD 26-04's remediation clock, even
though that paper predates BOD 26-04's issuance and doesn't name it.

## 5. CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model v2.0 — agency-facing maturity guidance, not a binding directive with its own deadline

**Who it binds:** no agency is legally required to hit a specific ZTMM
maturity stage by a specific date the way BOD 25-01 sets a hard deadline.
The Maturity Model — four stages, Traditional through Initial, Advanced, and
Optimal, across five pillars (Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications &
Workloads, Data) plus three cross-cutting capabilities (Visibility and
Analytics, Automation and Orchestration, Governance) — is CISA's own
maturity guidance, referenced by OMB M-22-09 as the framework agencies
should measure progress against, rather than itself the source of a
compliance deadline.

**What it means for agencies:** most federal Zero Trust programs stall below
Advanced maturity for structural reasons — pillar tools administered
independently rather than governed as one system, evidence that's per-tool
rather than per-claim, and Network/CSP/VMware estates assessed as three
disconnected exercises instead of one architecture. Buying another
per-pillar tool doesn't fix a structural stall; the companion papers below
argue this in depth, with named incidents (Storm-0558, the ESXiArgs
ransomware campaign, the VMware ESXi AD-integration bypass) as evidence, not
assertion.

**What it means for vendors:** CSP-native and third-party security tooling
vendors sell products that can *move* an agency along the maturity model,
but no vendor's tool, on its own, satisfies the model — that's the paper's
own central argument, not incidental to it.

**Read deeper:** [Zero Trust Governance
Principles](zero-trust-governance-principles.qmd) is the primary treatment;
its companion [Zero Trust Requires Whole-Agency
Scope](zero-trust-whole-agency-unification.qmd) covers why Network, every
CSP, and any on-premises virtualization estate have to be assessed as one
system. [Zero Trust Governance](zero-trust-governance-whitepaper.qmd) maps
the five pillars to specific canon-anchored mechanisms.

## 6. OMB M-22-09 (Federal Zero Trust Strategy) — the policy memo that makes ZTMM the reference standard

**Who it binds:** federal agencies. OMB Memorandum M-22-09 is the policy
instrument that directs agencies to adopt Zero Trust architecture principles
and use CISA's Zero Trust Maturity Model as the measurement framework — it's
the piece connecting §4's maturity model to an actual OMB-issued agency
obligation, rather than the maturity model being purely advisory.

**What it means for agencies:** M-22-09 is cited throughout this section
wherever a paper argues that a specific architectural move (application-aware
networking, phishing-resistant MFA, Conditional Access, SD-WAN local
breakout) is not optional best practice but a policy-driven expectation.

**What it means for vendors:** as with M-25-21 below, M-22-09 does not bind
vendors directly — it shapes what agencies procure, which shapes vendor
roadmaps indirectly.

**Read deeper:** [Federal Application Aware Networking
Architecture](federal-application-aware-networking-architecture.qmd) and its
UIAO-branded sibling [From Mainframe to Application-Aware
Modernization](modernization-journey.qmd) both build their core argument on
M-22-09's identity-and-application-aware-networking direction — see the
[Reading Guide](reading-guide.qmd) for which of the two fits your audience.

## 7. TIC 3.0 (OMB M-19-26) — agency-facing policy, satisfied through vendor infrastructure

**Who it binds:** federal agencies. OMB Memorandum M-19-26, *Update to the
Trusted Internet Connections (TIC) Initiative*, directs agencies to adopt
one of CISA's TIC 3.0 use cases for their network architecture, replacing
the prior single-hairpin TIC model. The obligation runs to the agency; the
means of satisfying it is almost always a vendor product (SD-WAN, SASE,
Direct Internet Access transport).

**What it means for agencies:** TIC 3.0 is the policy gate that makes Direct
Internet Access *lawful* for a distributed-egress architecture — but DIA on
its own satisfies none of the protection controls TIC 3.0 actually requires
(SC-7 boundary protection, SC-8 confidentiality, AC-4 flow enforcement, SI-3
malware protection). Those come from the SD-WAN/SASE governance stack layered
on top of the transport, not from the transport itself. An agency that reads
"TIC 3.0 allows DIA" and stops there — buying faster internet circuits
without the governance stack — has a compliance regression with better
latency, not modernization.

**What it means for vendors:** SD-WAN, SASE, and transport providers (fiber,
MPLS, LEO satellite, 5G) sell the infrastructure an agency uses to satisfy
TIC 3.0, but no vendor is itself bound by the directive — the compliance
obligation, and the accountability for it, stays with the agency regardless
of which vendor stack it procures.

**Read deeper:** [SD-WAN vs. DIA Under TIC 3.0](tic3-sdwan-vs-dia.qmd) is
the dedicated treatment — the "pipe vs. governor" argument, the physics
budget behind TIC 3.0's use cases, and the five-step decision sequence for
an actual transport/SD-WAN procurement. [Next Generation
DNS](infoblox-hybrid-dns-unified-ddi.qmd) covers the DNS-layer piece of the
same distributed-egress architecture.

## 8. OMB M-25-21 (Federal AI governance) — agency-facing, and the newest mandate in this set

**Who it binds:** federal agencies deploying or procuring AI systems. Per
[ADR-112](/docs/adr/adr-112-federal-ai-usecase-governance.html), OMB M-25-21
carries three binding obligations on the agency: an AI use-case inventory,
risk-tiered controls for "high-impact" AI use cases, and an accountable
official designated for each. It is the most recent mandate in this paper
and the one with the least field-tested guidance behind it.

**What it means for agencies:** an AI system has to be governed as an
identity-bearing, inventoried record — not just a model deployment — before
an ATO package involving AI can be considered complete under M-25-21's
terms. This is a live gap for most agencies: mature AI-inventory and
governance tooling for this specific mandate is newer than the tooling
maturity for FedRAMP, NIST, or BOD 25-01.

**What it means for vendors:** vendors selling AI capabilities into federal
agencies are not directly bound by M-25-21, but an agency's own compliance
posture increasingly depends on what inventory and governance hooks a
vendor's AI product exposes — an accountable official cannot govern what
isn't visible as a record.

**Read deeper:** [Federal AI Governance — Submission
Readiness](federal-ai-governance-submission-readiness.qmd) is the dedicated
treatment, including an honest coverage ledger of what's deployed versus
proposed against M-25-21's specific gates.

## Honest limits and scope {#honest-limits-and-scope}

- **This paper is a routing layer, not a primary source.** Every specific
  control number, deadline, and mechanism claim above is already cited, in
  more depth, by the companion paper it points to. Where this page and a
  companion paper appear to disagree, the companion paper is authoritative
  — this page should be corrected to match it, not the reverse.
- **Eight mandates, not the whole federal compliance clock — named, not
  silently dropped.** The Federal Organization Compliance (OrgComp) series
  this paper draws its FedRAMP timeline from tracks a materially larger set:
  BOD 18-01 (DMARC/HTTPS), BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation), BOD 23-01 (asset
  visibility), BOD 23-02 (management-interface exposure), OMB M-21-31
  (event logging), M-21-07 (IPv6), M-23-02 and NIST FIPS 203/204/205
  (post-quantum cryptography, migration through 2035), and NIST SP 800-53's
  own biannual minor-release cadence. None of those made the cut for this
  primer's eight sections — they're real, agency-facing, and out of scope
  here on length grounds, not because they don't matter. See the [OrgComp
  series' Executive
  Summary](../orgcomp-series/Vol_0_Book_00_OrgComp_Executive_Summary.qmd)
  for the fuller clock.
- **Scope is federal civilian, Moderate baseline.** DoD environments
  (IL4/IL5), state and local government compliance regimes, and
  non-federal commercial regulatory frameworks are out of scope. Several
  mandates above (FedRAMP in particular) have GCC-High and DoD-specific
  variants this paper does not address.
- **Dates are a snapshot.** The FedRAMP 20x timeline in §1 reflects the
  Consolidated Rules as published June 25, 2026; OMB and CISA guidance in
  this space has moved on shorter cycles than typical review cadences
  before. Verify current dates directly against FedRAMP.gov and CISA.gov
  before treating any date above as load-bearing for a procurement or
  ATO decision.
- **This is not legal or compliance advice.** It is a navigational aid for
  a specific, common confusion — which mandate binds which actor — not a
  substitute for an agency's own legal, compliance, or ISSO review of its
  specific posture against any mandate named here.
- **The three-actor model is a simplification.** Some real arrangements
  don't fit neatly — an agency operating its own GovCloud tenant is
  simultaneously acting in something closer to the CSP role for the
  systems it hosts there, and a systems integrator building on top of an
  authorized CSO for an agency client sits in a fourth position this
  paper doesn't model separately. Treat the three-actor framing as the
  common case, not an exhaustive taxonomy.

## Call to Action

::: {.callout-important}
## Four steps to start this quarter

1. **Sort your open compliance work items into "ours" and "our vendor's."**
   For each item currently tracked as a compliance obligation, name which
   actor in the Executive Summary's actor table it actually binds. Anything binding
   a CSP that your agency has been treating as agency work is effort you
   can redirect; anything binding your agency that's been assumed covered
   by a vendor's FedRAMP authorization is a gap to close now.
2. **Put the FedRAMP 20x dates on the calendar** — July 28 and August 3/31,
   2026, January 1 and June 11, 2027 — even though they're CSP-facing
   deadlines. Your agency's own SSP and reciprocity decisions for every
   FedRAMP-authorized CSO you rely on will need to reflect which side of
   those dates each vendor's authorization sits on.
3. **Pick the one mandate in §1-§8 that's most live for your agency right
   now** — the one with an open finding, an upcoming deadline, or a
   stalled program — and read that section's linked companion paper in
   full before the next planning cycle.
4. **If you're not sure which mandate applies to a specific open question,
   start with the actor, not the acronym.** Ask "is this something my
   agency does, or something our vendor does" before researching which
   framework governs it — the framework follows from the actor, and
   getting that backward is the single most common way this compliance
   landscape gets misread.
:::

None of this requires resolving every mandate at once. It requires knowing,
for each open compliance question, whether the answer starts with "we have
to" or "our vendor has to" — and reading the paper in this section that
actually goes deep on whichever one it turns out to be.
